description_good_justification: The README opens with what Workbench is and does: a control panel for every coding project on your computer that shows what needs attention across repos, starts and stops dev environments, and helps you pick up where you left off. https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench#readme
interact_justification: The README links to the latest release download and install steps, and its Feedback and contributing section says how to report bugs or ask for features (GitHub issues) and how to contribute (CONTRIBUTING.md). https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench#feedback-and-contributing
contribution_justification: CONTRIBUTING.md explains the process: fork, branch from main, open a pull request against main; required CI checks must pass before it can merge. https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md
contribution_requirements_justification: CONTRIBUTING.md lists what a change needs: tests, no ESLint or TypeScript (strict) errors or warnings, the security rules for request data and commands, a release note for user-visible changes, pinned actions, and dependency notes. https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#what-a-change-needs
documentation_basics_justification: docs/install.md (linked from the README) covers installing and starting it on macOS, Windows and Linux; docs/usage.md covers using every page; the README's Security section, SECURITY.md and docs/development.md cover using it securely (e.g. prefer the desktop app over npm run dev, which has no per-launch API token). https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/blob/main/docs/install.md
documentation_interface_justification: Workbench is a desktop app; its external interface is the UI, keyboard shortcuts, settings and files on disk. docs/usage.md documents the pages, keyboard shortcuts, preferences, what each action runs, how the projects folder is chosen (including WORKBENCH_PROJECTS_DIR) and every file in its data folder. The local HTTP API is internal to the app and refuses other callers. https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/blob/main/docs/usage.md
sites_https_justification: The project site, repository and release downloads are all on GitHub over HTTPS.
discussion_justification: GitHub issues and pull requests: searchable, addressable by URL, open to anyone with a GitHub account, and no proprietary client needed. https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/issues
english_justification: All documentation is in English, and bug reports and comments are accepted in English.
maintained_justification: Actively developed: five releases so far (https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/releases), weekly Dependabot updates, and issues and vulnerability reports are answered on GitHub.
repo_track_justification: Git on GitHub records every change, its author and its date.
repo_interim_justification: Every change since the first release landed on main through a public pull request, and every interim commit between releases is in the repository, not just the releases. https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/pulls
version_unique_justification: Each release has a unique version number (e.g. 0.1.4) in package.json, shown in the app's sidebar footer.
version_semver_justification: Semantic Versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH), set with npm version.
version_tags_justification: Each release is a git tag (v0.1.0 to v0.1.4 so far); pushing the tag runs the release workflow, and a ruleset stops release tags from being moved or deleted.
release_notes_justification: Every GitHub release has human-written notes for users (what's new, changed and fixed, and security fixes), maintained in src/lib/releaseNotes.ts, not a git log; the app also shows them under What's new. https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/releases
release_notes_vulns_justification: No publicly known vulnerabilities in Workbench have been fixed yet. The release notes would name any, with their CVE.
report_process_justification: Bug reports go to GitHub issues, as the README and CONTRIBUTING.md say. https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/issues
report_responses_justification: No bug reports have been submitted yet; reports are acknowledged on the issue tracker.
enhancement_responses_justification: No enhancement requests have been submitted yet; requests are answered on the issue tracker.
report_archive_justification: GitHub issues keep every report and response, searchable and public. https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/issues
vulnerability_report_process_justificati: SECURITY.md describes how to report a vulnerability, what to include, and which versions get fixes. https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/blob/main/SECURITY.md
vulnerability_report_private_justificati: Private vulnerability reporting is enabled; SECURITY.md links to the private report form (HTTPS). https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/security/advisories/new
vulnerability_report_response_justificat: No vulnerability reports have been received in the last 6 months.
build_justification: npm run build builds the app and npm run desktop:dist packages the desktop app; CI builds and launches the packaged app on macOS, Linux and Windows for every pull request. https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/blob/main/docs/development.md
build_common_tools_justification: npm scripts, Next.js, esbuild and electron-builder.
build_floss_tools_justification: Node.js, npm, Next.js, TypeScript, esbuild, Electron and electron-builder are all FLOSS; the Linux AppImages build with FLOSS tools only.
test_justification: A Vitest suite (1,350+ tests in src/**/*.test.ts, MIT like the project). Run it with npm test; docs/development.md lists the commands and CI runs it on every pull request. https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/blob/main/docs/development.md#commands
test_invocation_justification: npm test, the standard for Node.js projects.
test_most_justification: Coverage is about 99.9% of lines and 98.8% of branches, and CI fails if it drops below the floor in vitest.config.mts (85%).
test_continuous_integration_justificatio: GitHub Actions runs lint, typecheck and the tests with coverage on Linux, the tests on macOS and Windows, and the packaged app on all three, for every pull request and push to main. These are required checks for merging. https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci.yml
test_policy_justification: CONTRIBUTING.md: new functionality and bug fixes come with tests in the Vitest suite, and code that turns request data into paths or commands should also get a property-based test. https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#what-a-change-needs
tests_are_added_justification: Recent major features each came with tests: the Preferences view (6 test files), Containers page (4), Ports view (4) and Pull requests view (3). Coverage stays near 100%.
tests_documented_added_justification: The test policy is in CONTRIBUTING.md, under what a change needs. https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#what-a-change-needs
warnings_justification: ESLint (eslint-config-next core-web-vitals and TypeScript rules) and TypeScript in strict mode run in CI on every pull request.
warnings_fixed_justification: Lint and typecheck currently report 0 errors and 0 warnings, and must pass for a pull request to merge.
warnings_strict_justification: TypeScript strict mode is on, with Next's recommended and TypeScript ESLint rules; there is one eslint-disable comment in the code base.
know_secure_design_justification: The maintainer designed Workbench around these principles; SECURITY.md documents them. Fail-safe defaults and complete mediation: every API request passes one guard (src/proxy.ts) that refuses non-loopback hosts and, in the desktop app, requests without the per-launch token. Least privilege: workflows get read-only tokens, with write access only on the jobs that need it. Input validation with allowlists: project names must be bare folder names and file paths must resolve inside the project, through symlinks. Economy of mechanism and minimal attack surface: local only, no accounts, nothing hosted. Integrity: the desktop app checks its server files against SHA-256s recorded at build time.
know_common_errors_justification: The maintainer knows the common errors for a local web app that runs commands, and the code counters each one. OS command injection: commands run with execFile/spawn and fixed arguments, never a shell. Path traversal: allowlisted names and symlink-aware containment checks, with property-based tests. DNS rebinding and CSRF: Host checks and JSON-only writes that need a CORS preflight that is never approved. Missing authentication: a per-launch secret in the desktop app. XSS: React escaping, with Markdown rendered by react-markdown without raw HTML. Supply chain: actions pinned to SHAs, an action allowlist, Dependabot, npm audit and build provenance.
crypto_published_justification: Workbench uses only SHA-256 (to check its own files) and the operating system's CSPRNG through Node.js crypto. TLS is handled by git, the gh CLI, Node.js and Electron (Chromium).
crypto_call_justification: It calls Node.js's built-in crypto module and doesn't implement any cryptography itself.
crypto_floss_justification: Node.js crypto (OpenSSL) and Electron/Chromium (BoringSSL) are FLOSS.
crypto_keylength_justification: The per-launch API token is 256 bits of CSPRNG output and the hash is SHA-256. Workbench has no configurable key lengths; TLS settings are those of git, gh and Chromium.
crypto_working_justification: No broken algorithms or modes (MD4, MD5, DES, RC4, Dual_EC_DRBG, ECB) are used.
crypto_weaknesses_justification: No SHA-1 or CBC mode; SHA-256 only.
crypto_pfs_justification: Workbench implements no key agreement protocol. Its network connections are made by git, the gh CLI and Electron, whose TLS stacks negotiate forward-secret ciphers.
crypto_password_storage_justification: Workbench has no user accounts and stores no passwords.
crypto_random_justification: The only security secret, the per-launch API token, is crypto.randomBytes(32) (electron/main.ts), a CSPRNG. Math.random is used only for a decorative theme animation.
delivery_mitm_justification: Releases are downloaded from GitHub over HTTPS, and each file has a Sigstore-signed build-provenance attestation that can be checked with gh attestation verify. The in-app update check uses HTTPS, and the Windows updater verifies each update's SHA-512 from its feed.
delivery_unsigned_justification: SHA256SUMS is served only over HTTPS from GitHub releases, next to signed build-provenance attestations (also attached as workbench-<version>.intoto.jsonl from the release after 0.1.4); nothing is fetched over plain HTTP.
vulnerabilities_fixed_60_days_justificat: No open vulnerabilities: no security advisories, no open Dependabot alerts, and npm audit (run in CI on every change) reports none.
vulnerabilities_critical_fixed_justifica: Dependabot security updates are on, and REQUIREMENTS.md has the steps for shipping a security fix quickly; installed apps check for updates at launch and every 4 hours. https://github.com/mikegoforth/workbench/blob/main/REQUIREMENTS.md#shipping-a-security-fix
no_leaked_credentials_justification: GitHub secret scanning with push protection is on, with no alerts, and the desktop build fails if the server bundle picks up .env files.
static_analysis_justification: CodeQL (GitHub code scanning) analyzes the JavaScript/TypeScript and the workflows on every pull request and push, before any release; the main ruleset blocks merging with high or higher CodeQL security alerts. ESLint also runs in CI.
static_analysis_common_vulnerabilities_j: CodeQL's security queries check for common vulnerabilities such as path injection, command injection and XSS.
static_analysis_fixed_justification: No CodeQL alerts are open. Every alert so far (path injection) was either fixed or dismissed as a false positive with the reason recorded: names and paths are validated by resolveProjectDir and resolveFileIn, which are now property-tested.
static_analysis_often_justification: CodeQL runs on every pull request and every push to main.
dynamic_analysis_justification: Property-based tests (fast-check) run thousands of generated paths and project names through the functions that keep requests inside the projects folder, and CI launches the packaged desktop app on macOS, Linux and Windows (scripts/smoke-desktop.mjs). Both run on every change, so they run before every release.
dynamic_analysis_unsafe_justification: Workbench is written in TypeScript, a memory-safe language.
dynamic_analysis_enable_assertions_justi: The property-based tests assert invariants on every one of thousands of generated inputs, and the desktop smoke test asserts that the packaged server starts and the window loads.
dynamic_analysis_fixed_justification: No vulnerabilities have been found by dynamic analysis; a failing property test fails CI and blocks merging.
